title: The Spatial Experience of Visually Impaired and Blind: An Approach to Understanding the Importance of Multisensory Perception
research_focus: To understand how visually impaired and blind individuals experience and perceive the built environment through their compensatory senses, and to determine the spatial qualities that can enrich the multisensory experience in the built environment.

sample_context.description: 10 visually impaired and blind individuals (diverse in gender, age, type of impairment - early/late blind, and familiarity with visited places) participated in guided tours and semi-structured interviews. The autobiography 'The Days' by Taha Hussein, a congenitally blind author, was also analyzed as a source of remote/past experience.
sample_context.setting: A center for visually impaired and blind people (for interviews and guided tours), and the environments described in Taha Hussein's autobiography (rural Egypt, Al-Azhar University, Sorbonne France).

findings.antecedent: Built environment physical characteristics (volumetric configuration, geometric configuration, openings, building layout/orientation, object locations, materials/textures)
findings.consequent: Understanding of spatial structure, sense of enclosure, legibility, mental imagery, sense of position in space
findings.description: Visually impaired and blind individuals perceive various physical characteristics of the built environment (e.g., volume, geometry, materials) using their compensatory senses (haptic, auditory, olfactory, basic orientation systems), which helps them understand spatial structure and related qualities.

findings.antecedent: Differences in ceiling height, space proportions, finish floor material (carpeted/tiled)
findings.consequent: Perception of volumetric configuration (low/high ceiling, narrow/wide spaces), sense of spaciousness, spatial understanding, cognitive map construction (e.g., mosque imagery)
findings.description: Auditory cues, particularly reverberating echoes from footsteps and cane tapping, generated by variations in ceiling height, space proportions, and floor materials, enable visually impaired individuals to perceive the volumetric configuration of spaces and construct mental images.
supporting_quotes: “I think it has a higher ceiling... Same sense as I go to a mosque... I can feel it from the sound of my footsteps and tapping of my cane and even if it is silent, I can still sense the spaciousness ...same as walking in a narrow corridor is different than in a spacious space...”
“You can often tell how high a ceiling is by listening for the reverberation of a tap or a clap off the ceiling or the bounce-back off a distant wall”

findings.antecedent: Spatial organization, order, boundaries, different sounds, smells, movement rhythm, circulation network
findings.consequent: Perception of geometric configuration (e.g., lobby shape, symmetry), spatial and sequential cognitive map construction, orientation, navigation capacity
findings.description: Visually impaired individuals perceive the geometric layout and configuration of spaces through environmental references like spatial organization, order, boundaries, and associated sounds and smells. Movement rhythm and auditory/mobility cues are crucial for interpreting circulation and constructing cognitive maps.
supporting_quotes: “the overall shape of the lobby, I think it is like this...” and he started to use his hands that it is not straight and continued “umm it is like pentagon or hexagon.....”
“in the dorms that I was not that familiar with, in the ground level it had a lot of columns that I bump in...”

“in the past I used to depend on my capacity to see light and dark but now since I no more do, I start to move around and focus more on my hearing sense to be able to interpret the shape of the route I should be taking and get more familiar with the space...”

“...but at a certain point ... he caught the confused sound of conversation through a half-open door on the left; then he knew that a pace or two further on he must turn to the left up a staircase which would bring him to his lodging.”

findings.antecedent: Natural elements (sun heat intensity/direction, wind/breeze flow/direction), contextual vegetation smell-scape
findings.consequent: Perception of window location, scale, and size; building orientation; construction of mental images (time of day, season, ambience, beautiful scenery)
findings.theme_name: Opening Size and Location/ Building Orientation
findings.description: Haptic and olfactory cues from natural elements like sun heat, wind flow, and vegetation smells enable visually impaired individuals to perceive the location, size, and orientation of openings and the overall building orientation, contributing to vivid mental imagery and sense of ambience.
supporting_quotes: “...feeling sunlight heat so I start to know that there is a window in that place ....like this room we are in now. I know now that the window is on my right.....and here at the staircase there is sunlight... I always felt the heat of the sun coming from high above.”

“For me I don't see light, but I feel heat from the sun ...So for example the very first time I entered my apartment I knew its orientations from the heat coming from each side... walls and windows...”
“Since it was surrounded by a lot of plants and looked so beautiful ...it was the smell of basil and a lot of plants and flowers and mint that helped me draw this image in my mind”
“the most picture I still have in my mind about that house till present is the natural scenery and tranquility no pollution no sound of cars.”

“To the best of his belief, the time of day was either dawn or dusk. That is due to the fact that he remembers feeling a slightly cold breeze on his face, which the heat of the sun had not destroyed... he did not feel around him any great movement of people stirring, but he only felt the movement of people waking from sleep or settling down to it.”

findings.antecedent: Air flow changes, different floor materials near obstacles, returning contextual soundscape (echoes), presence of other individuals
findings.consequent: Detection of dynamic and static obstacles, sense of safety and security, orientation and navigation skills
findings.description: Visually impaired individuals detect obstacles using haptic cues (air flow changes), auditory cues (echoes from surrounding environment, sounds of others), and tactile cues (cane tapping on different floor materials), enhancing their safety, orientation, and navigation.
supporting_quotes: “I think this is a partition...too annoying... I think they should have done anything before that partition in the floor material so it can help me avoid it ...also the thickness of the partition is so thin, sometimes the cane can help me know its place. but in other cases it is quite difficult.”
“I think I feel it because of the difference in air flow”

findings.antecedent: Surface materials (texture, felt weight, temperature, smell), floor contour (steps, slopes, bumps), auditory cues from footsteps/cane
findings.consequent: Recognition of material type, construction of mental images (e.g., staircase of mud, drowsiness environment), sense of happiness, sense of position in space, navigation and orientation skills, sense of accessibility/confinement
findings.description: Visually impaired individuals perceive material qualities (texture, temperature, smell, sound reflection) and floor contours through multisensory engagement (haptic, auditory, motion), which aids in material recognition, mental imagery, emotional responses, and spatial navigation.
supporting_quotes: “It was an ordinary sort of staircase, ... and its steps were of stone; but since it was used very frequently in both directions, and no one troubled to wash or sweep it, the dirt piled up thickly and stuck together in a compact mass on the steps, so that the stone was completely covered up, and whether you were going up or coming down the staircase appeared to be made of mud...”
“...also through the sound of others footsteps, I started also to know even the fine details of the place such as the type of materials of flooring...”

“How happy he was when he put off his shoes at the door of the mosque and walked first on the straw-mat, then on the marble and then on the thin carpet, which was spread over the floor of the mosque. How happy he was when he took his place among the circle on this carpet by the side of a marble pillar. He touched the pillar and liked its glossy smoothness,”

“... if there has remained to him any clear distinct memory it is the memory of a fence which stood in front of him and was made of maize stems and which was only a few paces away from the door of the house. He remembers the fence as though he saw it only yesterday. He remembers that the stalks of which this fence were composed were taller than he was and it was difficult for him to get to the other side of it..........He also recalls that the stalks of this fence were close together, as it were stuck together, so that he could not squeeze between them.”

“while going back to the dorm, first after going out of the door I go down the pedestrian walk way then move forward until I meet another step and move forward I feel grass beneath my feet then from here I understand that I arrived... that's because I memorize the place very good.”

“I know where is my exact location for example by knowing how many speed bumps I passed.....if I passed this bridge where will I reach....For example when I skip "Banha” I know it when there is a certain bridge with a certain feeling while I go down its slope ...”

derived_hypotheses: Architectural design that incorporates multisensory cues (auditory, haptic, olfactory) related to volumetric and geometric configurations, natural elements, obstacle detection, and material qualities will enhance spatial understanding, navigation, and mental imagery for both sighted and visually impaired individuals.
Implementing different sensible materials for surfaces at the beginning and end of pedestrian crossings can improve obstacle detection for visually impaired individuals.
Spatial organization that considers rhythm of movement, auditory, and olfactory perception can enhance the experience of the built environment.
mechanism_candidates: Compensatory Senses: In the absence of vision, other senses (haptic, auditory, olfactory, basic orientation) are enhanced and utilized to gather information about the built environment.
Sensory Stimulants: Physical characteristics of the built environment act as sensory stimulants, producing distinct cues (e.g., reverberating echoes, air flow changes, material textures, smells).

Cognitive Processing: Perceived sensory information from these stimulants aids in cognitive processes such as constructing mental imagery, forming cognitive maps (spatial and sequential), and supporting orientation and navigation.
Spatial Landmarks: Differences in volumetric configuration, geometric layout, and material qualities act as spatial landmarks for orientation and navigation.
Embodied Experience: Movement through space, combined with haptic and auditory feedback, contributes to the perception of spatial dimensions and configurations.
transferability_limits: The study was conducted in a specific cultural context (Egypt, with Taha Hussein's autobiography describing rural Egypt and Cairo).
The small sample size (10 participants) limits the generalizability of the findings.
The study focused primarily on touch, smell, and hearing, with other sensory channels like taste not significantly addressed.
limitations: Other sensory channels such as taste and smell were not significantly addressed in this study.
The study could benefit from engaging more data collection sources such as autobiographies for other sensory disabilities, personal reflections, and documentation of films featuring sensory issues.
